edges.description: The splice-donor variant disrupts splicing of the skin-specific transcript.
Reduced skin-specific SMARCAD1, a chromatin remodeller, is presumed to impair chromatin remodelling in developing epidermis (inferred; the mechanism is described as unclear in the primary sources).

nodes.description: Beyond the ridge defect, deficiency of the skin-specific isoform produces an ectodermal-dysplasia phenotype affecting the epidermis and its appendages: transient congenital facial milia, rapidly healing neonatal acral bullae, reduced eccrine sweating, and nail dystrophy. The specific developmental mechanism tying these appendage defects to SMARCAD1 loss is not established and is inferred here from the shared causal variant.

evidence.reference_title: Basan gets a new fingerprint: Mutations in the skin-specific isoform of SMARCAD1 cause ectodermal dysplasia syndromes with adermatoglyphia.
evidence.snippet: Basan syndrome is an autosomal dominant ectodermal dysplasia (ED) with congenital adermatoglyphia, transient neonatal acral bullae, and congenital facial milia.

nodes.description: Congenital absence of the epidermal ridges (dermatoglyphs) on the fingers, palms, toes, and soles, so that fingerprints are absent. This is the defining feature and gives the syndrome its "immigration delay disease" alias through failed fingerprint-based identification.

Reduced protein level is inferred from the RNA-level data.

nodes.description: A heterozygous variant affecting the skin-specific short isoform of SMARCAD1, which begins with an alternative, otherwise-noncoding first exon. In almost all reported families the variant is a point mutation in the donor splice site of that alternative exon 1; one family instead carries a large structural variant (a deletion with nontandem inverted duplication) that removes the first nine exons including the skin-isoform exon 1. SMARCAD1 is a SNF2-family chromatin remodeller.

evidence.snippet: Sequencing of all SMARCAD1 coding and noncoding exons revealed a heterozygous transversion predicted to disrupt a conserved donor splice site adjacent to the 3' end of a noncoding exon uniquely present in the skin-specific short isoform of the gene.
